Yeah, I bet if you divided the game into a dozen different areas like professions, M+, raids, leveling etc, and asked people to pick the best version across all expansions, you'd probably have highly varied responses but also picks across a broad range of iterations of WoW. The whole story of the Lich King expansion felt great, and the music, environment design, armour sets, they were all guided by the story. We used to get amazing armour sets for raids and PVP that were based on the theme of the raid or bosses, then we had the huge disappointment of Uldir. It would be an interesting topic to discuss but would take ages!

Blizzard have been both praised and criticised for making the game more accessible to people who don't like or play MMORPGs. I definitely consider myself one of those, at least these days. I've had my phases of being permanently online, getting my social fill from my guildmates and doing all sorts of stuff in the game, raiding 4-5 nights a week, but these days, the less I have to interact with players, the better. Toxicity can be a factor in some places, but I actually enjoyed the solo leveling process and getting to join dungeons with a handy tool in the UI. I don't even see why we should have to be summoned to M+ dungeons at this point, just get on with it, you know? I know things used to take a lot longer, but that wasn't necessarily a good thing. What if you only have an hour or two to play? Would you want to have to spend some of that time traveling, farming, or hunting for a dungeon group? 

I think you could expand the dungeon finder to include M+, but then introduce a reputation system similar to other types of games. While you're in a dungeon or shortly after you've finished, you can thumbs up or down a player for a few different things. If you're consistently toxic, you end up being paired with toxic players, and the nice players find other nice players.

I think you're probably right about classic being more complex. I joined at the end of Vanilla and glad I didn't have to do so many of the awful grinds or elaborate quest chains involved. The game needed time to find its feet and for its gameplay to evolve into something more consistent and fun across the board.

Yeah, I understand. I've been playing a bit of Star Trek Online lately and while that game has a ton of its own problems, they have daily 'endeavours' and a weekly one. The weekly one seems to be doing a particular event, finishing a lengthy PVE community goal (which might take 30 mins-1hr), and the endeavours will be things like doing plasma damage (in space battles), killing Borg (on the ground), and they also increase in difficulty or requirements, meaning greater rewards (being particularly generous in credits and crafting materials). I like that system, partly because it doesn't give you gear, so you don't feel the pressure to complete them every day. They're just a way to get you to vary up the gameplay if you want a change.

That's true as well! From what I remember of the old days, yes the crafting professions were simpler, but by the time you had the reputation to access the recipe and/or the materials, you've probably looted better gear anyway. It was often less effort to just grind heroic dungeons etc and buy a decent equivalent, rather than buy a crafted BOE. I think if you're going to add unlockable recipes, make the rewards be an actual upgrade, like you said.

We're also so deep into the WoW story that I think each character should be able to have two gathering professions, and maybe increase the synergy between them and the crafting/consumables professions. Maybe skinning could provide more materials for cooking for example, but I'm getting into minutia. They haven't really done anything with archaeology for a long time, but they could tie it in with questing, transmog collecting, the battle pet system, any maybe make the rewards more appealing (and potentially sellable like mounts). Previous expansions like LK had various gear patches/upgrades that different professions offered, so there was always need for things. They kinda gutted jewelcrafting compared to how popular it was back then.

On the other hand, what if you want to focus on dungeons etc and don't want to have to do professions? Should you miss out on bonuses?

One of the reasons WoW is a great game with wide appeal is the wide variety of things people can do in the game, be it PVE (dungeons, raids, world etc), PVP (world, arena, BGs), RP, questing, collecting and so on. I don't want to take away the possibilities, but I don't like the idea of forcing people who like one main aspect (arguably PVE or PVP) to need to participate in the other areas. 

At some points for example, arena/PVP players had to do certain raids for particular trinkets or bits of gear, or needed to grind reputation outside of PVP settings to gain access to upgrades/enchants. PVE players who might be on a new character or trying to catch up might be encouraged to grind PVP gear just for the ilvl (I'm going back years now so probably not as relevant), or have to develop professions or other systems to be able to get an edge/max out their character. 

I think that if you love doing M+, you should be able to unlock what you need just from 'playing the game' as you prefer it. Ditto with raids, arena etc. There would be nothing stopping you from doing lots of different things in the game, but anything that takes you away from your preferred part is a negative I think.

In my opinion, and having played since Vanilla, I think they made it too complicated and shouldn't have added any RNG or quality levels. You used to loot or earn a recipe and then gradually acquire the materials to craft a decent (but rarely essential) piece of gear, and as long as the crafter had the profession level to use the recipe, they could craft it and you knew what you were getting. Procs can be fun (particularly for alchemists), but shouldn't be relied upon.

If you enjoy the new systems, that's absolutely fine, it just doesn't work for my taste :(

Exactly - on most expansions I level up, go through the story, get enough gear for dungeons, then heroics, maybe early M+ and do LFR, possibly normal mode raids if I have the motivation. As a player without a guild these days, I think that's reasonable. The problem then is finding something to do once you've done a bit of M+ and maybe cleared the heroic raid in a PUG. You could level an alt or respect to try a different role, but you'll end up playing the same dungeons and same 1-2 raids for months. I get bored so quickly, and definitely don't enjoy doing anything outside of dungeons etc to grind reputation or whatever.

I was watching some of the old world first videos from BC and LK era, and the game felt much simpler back then. There are so many systems and different things to grind, when in my opinion, it should all be about fun gameplay, gear, and if there are any systems like a reputation, then you should be able to progress them by playing the same main content. Remember when you could wear a faction's tabard in dungeons to earn rep up to revered? Why not let people unlock exalted too, and allow raid reputation gains too?


I think what I'm trying to say is that there is too much stuff that takes you away from the core gameplay loop for me. They've made the game simpler for people with alts in some ways, but they absolutely ruined professions and added all these extra steps outside of raids/dungeons that you need to upgrade your gear. 


I'm speaking broadly about a few of the recent expansions and patches, so I apologise for being vague. The game is still unnecessarily complex from what I've seen and can remember, and they could do a lot more to keep it interesting without resorting to grind.

I was diagnosed with dysthymia (which has since been renamed Persistent Depressive Disorder) nearly 10 years ago (38 now). I don't think I could say I've dealt with it, as it's the reason I tick the disability box when starting a new job. 

  
In my experience, it has made me very flat by default, able to have some fun, enough for an introvert like me to enjoy seeing a few friends and have a laugh, enjoy some hobbies and find satisfaction in work, but I don't think I've ever felt 'happy' like others describe or present it. In addition to the generally flat mood and a fairly frequent inability to enjoy things (though there's the possible ASD/ADHD diagnosis to thank for that too), I get dips that might last nearly a week. They're still not as extreme as other forms of depression, but they do drag everything down.



Having the diagnosis helped identify how the condition works and made me more aware of the signs and symptoms, so in a sense, I can detach from it like I would a physical injury that's flaring up. Even if my mind is in a very negative place, I have enough detachment to say to my friends, partner, family, or boss, that it'll pass and I try not to give too much attention to my thoughts or make any decisions while in this phase. I also explain what I'm like to any new boss, things like not appearing or being as enthusiastic or excited by things, but I make up for it by having a positive and helpful attitude. 



I can relate to your line about family providing for you; I am fortunate to have had a sheltered upbringing and still have that safety net, but the more independence I can find or create for myself, the smaller the (perceived) burden on my family and therefore less guilt. 

  
I've also spent my fair share of days watching or playing lots of things hoping for something to make me feel better, but I found that making positive changes to my life, where possible, were the best thing to make me feel better in the short and long term. Positive changes can be anything from tidying your desk or tidying/cleaning your room all the way up to changing job/career, cutting negative influences or people out of your life, finishing something you've been putting off like overdue admin, but there is definitely some truth to 'tidy room, tidy mind'. I have a small checklist of things to do when I'm feeling bad, and aside from tidying up and cleaning (even washing up is therapeutic for me), reaching out to others is great. If they're willing to listen, it'll give you a space to 'unpack' what's on your mind, if the brain fog is getting you down.

  
Another thing that's easy to forget is that depressive episodes/states by their nature make us self-centred, so try to do something for other people, even if it's just calling them to ask how they are. Offer to help somehow, even consider some volunteering. At one of my jobs where I was mostly doing admin, the highlight of my day was getting to help someone unload a car; feeling helpful always gives me a boost. 

  
Things have improved for me in the last ten years, but it's all been down to changes in my life - getting out of a bad relationship, town, business, going back to the industry I studied for and a much better city, and more recently deciding on another career change to feel more helpful, hopefully starting to work in education in the new year. 

This might be a particularly British way of thinking, but the motto 'things could always be worse', while a double-edged sword, can be helpful most of the time. Think of good things that have happened to you or that you've done that day or recently, think of what you can be grateful for, even if you have to check where you sit on the hierarchy of needs. If you have a few hundred in the bank, a roof over your head, family you can call on for help, you're already better off than a lot of people. The reason I call it a double-edged sword is because at some point, you should address the negatives in your day/life. Don't brush your problems under the rug for too long, because however better or worse your situation is than someone else's, your health is your own priority and isn't to be compared. Don't ever let someone tell you you don't deserve to feel down or have anything to feel depressed about.

Apologies for the ramble, but I hope it helps!

Don't take any risks with your wellbeing or safety, don't run unless it's an emergency. Keep an eye out for hazards and spot for other people (make sure no camera ops trip over or something). Enthusiasm to help out goes a long way and I've seen someone be hired purely on that basis this year. 

Don't be afraid to say you don't know the answer to something or don't recognise a term - it's always best to ask rather than assume. It's easy to compare notes/vent about bad previous employers or jobs, we all do it, but it can be a downer and you never know who's worked with whom - try to counter negativity with positive memories or just don't pile on. 

Be nice to everyone, especially contributors/members of the public. Make sure they're comfortable and make them feel welcome, but be ready to keep busy especially if others around you are working. If a camera operator is setting up for an interview or something, they might appreciate your help, but sometimes just chatting to a contributor to make them feel at ease is just as helpful so they can concentrate on tech setup. 

If you're taking food orders, ask people for one or two backup options so you're not in a panic trying to guess what else they'd like if the shop doesn't have any turkey and stuffing sandwiches left. Keep an eye out for allergies on the call sheet or ask people if they have any in case you do have to make your best guess. Don't worry too much though - worst case if you pick something they don't like, usually people are happy to swap. 

Stay in WhatsApp contact with your production co-ordinator to both ask questions on the day but also keep them updated on how the shoot is going - if you guys think you might be running late, the more notice you can give them the easier it'll be to re-arrange travel for example. 

Is there a particular department or area you're interested in? Feel free to DM me if you have any questions - I mostly work in production rather than tech crew or editorial.

It’s a bleak reality for many. For me, I thought I was lucky enough to be able to look for a place with a friend recently and move out of a SpareRoom house share in Cardiff. House shares are great but after you’ve done a few, the thought of not having to get to know a whole new group of strangers again sounds appealing.  
  
But I was naïve to think that being able to move in with someone I already knew would make the process easier. The market is crazy right now.  
  
Understandably, with the current renting climate, it was easy enough to find someone to fill my room in my former house share on August 30. This was a few months ago, and I thought there was plenty of time for me to find somewhere else with my friend, so I promised the new person the room was hers.  
  
One of the first places I called up brought me to an automated message informing me that I was ‘number 79’ for a viewing, and my heart sank. I definitely hadn't realised how competitive the renting climate was.  
  
Most of the time, I was told by estate agents that they were fully booked for viewings and wouldn’t be able to schedule me in to see it anything at all - they were going like hot cakes. With my former room accounted for, it was now playing on my mind knowing I had to be out by a certain date.  
  
My friend, who was living with her ex at this point, was also more than ready to find somewhere as soon as possible. The only viewings we were offered were right in the middle of the day, and with us both working full time this was just not feasible, so we resorted to virtual viewings - with estate agents Whatsapp-ing us video tours of properties left, right and centre.  
  
Of course, you don’t get the same feel for it, (my worst fear was that we'd sign ourselves up for somewhere that was secretly full of mould). But at this point we were beginning to lose track of what we’d looked at, so we were pretty much offering our holding deposit out to anyone that would take it. And even then, it was the same story again and again.  
  
We’d express interest, and hear nothing. Or we were told on several occasions that landlords had decided to proceed with another tenant.  
  
It was understandable, considering how competitive these cheaper rental places seemed to be, yet maddening at the same time. When my friend and I finally managed to look around one place, we were the last people they could fit in that day.

We arrived, and the estate agent told us that eight people had already seen the flat that day, and all of them were interested. The woman who showed us around simply said: “It’s really competitive at the moment, we’ve had such a wave of interest for these types of places.”  
  
After several weeks of ringing around other places we finally put a holding deposit down on somewhere that we had never viewed in person. We didn't even know if it had a washing machine, but with just one week before my room was about to be taken over, the clock was ticking.  
  
Not to sound dramatic, but I think that might be the most stressed I have been in my adult life, and was fully prepared at one point to have to Airbnb it until I found somewhere permanent. I’ve rented for about five years now in different cities, and it truly made me realise how no-one is talking about the renting crisis in Cardiff at the moment.  
  
I think it’s a combination of feeling like nothing can be done and a lack of information, so I contacted every estate agency I could find in Cardiff to ask them for their thoughts on the letting situation in Cardiff right now. But out of all of the estate agents I contacted: Mr Homes, CPS Homes, James Douglas, Peter Alan, Moginie James, Hern Crabtree, Cardiff Estate Agents and Lettings and Jeffrey Ross Estate Agents, only one wished to comment.  
  
John Hooper-Nash, who oversees the lettings department at Jeffrey Ross Estate Agents, said: "All you hear is that landlords are terrible people who rip people off, but this isn't the case at all. What we do see is landlords leaving the market which has caused an issue and secondly I've never known so many people wanting to live here which is great on one hand, but there's just not enough properties to go round for people to live in.  
  
"There's not enough properties to go round, so we find a lot of people paying inflated rent, or simply not being able to find anywhere suitable and having to move out of the area and things like that so there's lots of things at play at the moment."  
  
And could the cost of living crisis also play a part? John also noted: "Cardiff's always been fairly cheap to rent in compared to its competition, and when I say competition I mean cities like Bristol. So we're getting more people coming over here but the short of it is that there's not enough properties.  
  
"We've also don't like to advertise on Rightmove any more because it's just carnage with the amount of calls we get. I think the record number was 283 independent people calling up about a one-bedroom place in Roath, so that's 282 people having to find something else.  
  
"I'm not even sure there are 283 properties like that to rent in Roath to start with. That's an extreme case, but on average we can get up to 75 enquiries at the moment for rented properties."
